title: Preoperative Gait Speed as a Predictor of Patient-Reported Outcomes After Total Hip Arthroplasty
journal: The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery
breakthrough: In 274 patients followed after primary THA for osteoarthritis, preoperative 10-metre free gait speed was a significant independent predictor of midterm patient-reported outcomes. A preoperative speed of 1.0 m/s separated those who reached the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (Oxford Hip Score ≥42, Forgotten Joint Score-12 ≥50) from those who did not, and the threshold held regardless of age.
impact: Supports adding a timed walk to the standard preoperative workup alongside the questionnaires. Gait speed is a two-minute measurement that captures function a PROM asks the patient to estimate.
practical: Use it to flag the patient likely to be dissatisfied and to justify prehabilitation before an elective hip. Read the design before quoting it: this is a retrospective cohort, Level III prognostic evidence, in a single Asian population. It shows that slow walkers do worse, not that making them faster changes the outcome — no prehabilitation trial has tested the threshold.
link: JBJS — preoperative gait speed and PROMs after THA

verify.status: corrected — study design, publication year and the strength of the claim
verify.note: Real study, correctly identified. THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) Design: submitted as a 'prospective clinical study'; it is a retrospective cohort of 274 patients operated 2012-2018, Level III prognostic. (2) Date: published in JBJS on 4 March 2026, not 2025. (3) The submitted phrase 'the single most reliable predictor of long-term postoperative satisfaction' overstates it — the paper reports gait speed as a significant predictor among several preoperative variables (symptom duration, pain intensity, hip range of motion, muscle strength), and the outcome window is midterm, not long-term. Added the PASS cut-offs and the point that a prognostic association is not evidence prehabilitation works, which is how this result will be misused.

title: Physical Therapy Adds Nothing to Structured Home Exercise in Meniscal Tear with Knee Osteoarthritis (TeMPO)
breakthrough: 879 patients aged 45 to 85 with knee pain, osteoarthritis and a degenerative meniscal tear were randomised across four arms: a 3-month structured home-exercise programme alone, home exercise plus adherence text messages, home exercise plus texts plus sham in-clinic physical therapy, and home exercise plus texts plus standard in-clinic physical therapy. All four groups improved substantially. Adding supervised physical therapy produced no meaningful additional pain relief at 3 months — the difference versus home exercise alone was 2.5 points and was not statistically significant.
impact: Reinforces non-operative management as first line over early arthroscopic debridement or meniscectomy, and goes further: the effective ingredient is the exercise, not the supervision. Adherence texting and in-clinic attendance both failed to add benefit.
practical: A structured home programme is a complete first-line treatment, not a compromise for patients who cannot get to therapy. Reserve in-person PT for patients who need manual therapy, cannot exercise unsupervised, or are not improving. Note this is a 3-month outcome in a 4-arm trial run at Brigham and Women's, Buffalo, Cleveland Clinic and Pittsburgh.
link: NEJM — A Randomized Trial of Physical Therapy for Meniscal Tear and Knee Pain

verify.status: REVERSED — the result was submitted in the opposite direction
verify.note: Real trial (TeMPO, NEJMoa2503385, 29 Oct 2025, n=879). THE FINDING WAS STATED BACKWARDS. The submission says supervised physical therapy offered 'modest additional benefit over self-directed home exercise programs alone'. The trial found the opposite: no meaningful additional pain relief from standard PT, sham PT or adherence texts on top of home exercise, difference 2.5 points and not significant. This is a negative trial and its clinical value is precisely that it is negative — rewritten to say so, with the four arms named so the reader can see what was actually compared.

title: 2025 AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Rotator Cuff Injuries
breakthrough: The AAOS replaced its 2019 rotator cuff guideline with 21 recommendations and eight options. The emphasis of the update is the healing environment rather than the indication for surgery: a strong recommendation now supports bioinductive implants during repair to reduce retear and improve patient-reported outcomes; routine acromioplasty is not suggested alongside arthroscopic repair of small-to-medium full-thickness tears; and MRI, MR arthrography, CT and ultrasound are all endorsed as adjuncts to examination and radiographs for identifying tears.
impact: Moves the guideline conversation from whether to repair towards how to make a repair hold. The acromioplasty statement withdraws support for a step still performed reflexively in many repairs.
practical: Two changes alter what you do this week: consider a bioinductive implant in a repair at risk of retear, and stop adding acromioplasty to a small-to-medium full-thickness repair for therapeutic benefit. Imaging choice is a matter of availability rather than accuracy.
link: AAOS — updated CPG for the management of rotator cuff injuries

verify.status: corrected — the guideline is real, the described content was not its emphasis
verify.note: The guideline exists and the date is right: AAOS Board approved it in August 2025, replacing the 2019 version, with 21 recommendations and 8 options. CORRECTION TO CONTENT. The submission describes it as clarifying conservative care versus early repair and establishing 'treatment pathways based on tear etiology, patient age, tissue quality, and symptom duration'. That is not what the 2025 update is about — AAOS's own summary frames it around optimising the healing environment: biologics, bioinductive implants, retear reduction, acromioplasty and imaging. Rewritten to the recommendations that were actually published, since the submitted version would have a resident quoting decision criteria the guideline does not contain.

title: Perioperative Opioid Counseling Before ACL Reconstruction (Randomized Controlled Trial)
journal: The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery
breakthrough: 121 patients undergoing ACL reconstruction were randomised 1:1 to opioid-limiting perioperative pain education — take opioids only as a last resort — or to conventional counselling to take opioids as needed for severe pain and 'stay ahead of the pain'. Within 3 months the last-resort group used a median of 15 mg of oxycodone versus 53 mg in the control group (mean total morphine equivalents 46.0 versus 63.6 mg, p < 0.001). Mean pain on the numeric rating scale over the first 14 days was 2.5 versus 2.4 (p = 0.82), with similar sleep quality and satisfaction.
impact: Direct randomised evidence that how the prescription is framed, not just how large it is, drives consumption. Supports standardised preoperative pain education as a formal step in outpatient sports medicine and arthroscopy.
practical: The intervention is a script, not a drug or a device, and it costs nothing. Counsel opioids as a rescue rather than a schedule, and expect roughly a two-thirds reduction in what the patient takes with no change in reported pain. Single-centre, 121 patients — large enough for the consumption endpoint, not powered for rare harms.
link: JBJS — perioperative opioid counseling for patients undergoing ACL reconstruction

verify.note: Verified and accurate as submitted, including the 15 mg versus 53 mg median oxycodone figures and the absence of any pain or satisfaction penalty. Randomised trial of 121 patients at the University of Maryland Rehabilitation & Orthopaedic Institute, JBJS 16 July 2025. Two small precisions added rather than corrected: the trial is labelled perioperative (not purely preoperative) counselling, and the mean total morphine equivalents (46.0 versus 63.6 mg) are quoted alongside the medians because the medians make the effect look larger than the means do. Sample size stated so the entry does not read as definitive on safety.

title: 2025 AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline Update: Management of Acute Compartment Syndrome
breakthrough: The five-yearly review of the AAOS acute compartment syndrome guideline was released. This is a minor update: one recommendation changed — the strength of evidence for Associated Fracture moved from Consensus (one star) to Limited (two stars) — with new supporting evidence added and the remaining recommendations unchanged.
impact: Confirms rather than revises the existing framework for diagnosing and treating acute compartment syndrome in traumatised extremities. The value of reading it is knowing which of your practices rest on consensus and which now have limited evidence behind them.
practical: Applies to adults with extremity trauma. It cannot be extrapolated to children or adolescents, and it does not address chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Do not expect new pressure thresholds or fasciotomy timing rules from this edition — the underlying evidence base has not changed enough to produce them, which is itself the message.

verify.status: corrected — real guideline, the scope of the update was overstated
verify.note: The 2025 update is real and the date is right (published 18 November 2025). CORRECTION. The submission claims it 'offers refined diagnostic parameters and surgical thresholds' and 'standardizes diagnostic protocols, continuous intracompartmental pressure monitoring criteria, and urgency timelines for surgical fasciotomy'. AAOS describes the opposite: a routine five-year review that 'received minor adjustments, primarily in the form of a single updated recommendation and the addition of supporting evidence', the single change being the Associated Fracture recommendation moving from Consensus to Limited. Rewritten to what changed, and the scope limits (adults only, not chronic exertional) added because both are stated explicitly in the guideline.

title: The "Quiet Knee" Rehabilitation Protocol After Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty
journal: The Journal of Arthroplasty / AAHKS Annual Meeting
breakthrough: A retrospective cohort from the Hospital for Special Surgery compared a supervised 10-day 'quiet knee' protocol — limited passive range of motion, restricted ambulation, aggressive cryotherapy and oedema control with telerehabilitation oversight — against conventional hands-on aggressive rehabilitation after primary TKA. Opioid exposure was lower with the quiet knee: 52.5 versus 67.5 inpatient morphine milligram equivalents and 265.5 versus 332.1 MME over 90 days after discharge, a reduction of more than 25%. In adjusted models conventional rehabilitation used 15 MME more as an inpatient and 58 MME more after discharge. Length of stay was shorter, with no detriment to pain, function or major complications.
impact: Challenges the assumption that immediate aggressive range of motion is required after knee replacement. Rest and swelling control early did not cost motion later in this cohort.
practical: Worth trialling in patients who struggle with early therapy pain, provided motion is tracked so a genuinely stiffening knee is still caught. Read this as an association: it is a retrospective cohort, not a randomised comparison, so the protocol travelled with a whole care pathway and the opioid difference cannot be attributed to the rehabilitation alone.
link: Quiet knee rehabilitation after primary TKA — retrospective cohort

verify.status: corrected — design and one outcome that was not measured
verify.note: Real: HSS, presented at the AAHKS annual meeting and published as 'Quiet Knee Rehabilitation Protocol After Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty Is Associated With Lower Opioid Exposure and No Added Risks: A Retrospective Cohort Study'. The 25% opioid reduction is accurate and the MME figures are quoted from the paper. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Design: submitted as a 'clinical evaluation... demonstrated that shifting... significantly reduced'; it is retrospective and the paper's own title says 'associated with'. (2) The submission claims it 'significantly reduced surgical site inflammation' — oedema control is part of the protocol, not a measured outcome; the reported outcomes were opioid exposure, length of stay, pain, function and complications. That claim removed.

title: Surgery vs Functional Bracing for Closed Displaced Humeral Shaft Fractures (FISH)
date: May 2020, with prespecified secondary analyses since
breakthrough: 82 adults with closed, displaced humeral shaft fractures were randomised at two Finnish university trauma centres to open reduction and plate fixation (n = 38) or functional bracing (n = 44). Function measured by DASH did not differ meaningfully between groups. The real separation was healing: 14 of the 44 braced patients developed healing problems requiring secondary surgery, and those who crossed over late had inferior outcomes out to two years compared with patients fixed at the outset.
impact: Reframes the humeral shaft decision. It is not a choice between a better and a worse functional result; it is a choice between accepting a roughly one-in-three chance of needing an operation later and having that operation now, with the knowledge that the delayed operation does worse.
practical: Counsel bracing as a reasonable first choice with an explicit non-union rate, and set a follow-up schedule that catches failure early rather than late. In a patient in whom a second anaesthetic or a delayed recovery would be especially costly, the crossover data are the argument for primary fixation — not any claimed early functional advantage.
link: JAMA — the FISH randomized clinical trial

verify.status: corrected — journal, year and the direction of the functional result
verify.note: The trial is real (FISH, Finnish Shaft of the Humerus, enrolled Nov 2012 to Jan 2018, 82 randomised). THREE CORRECTIONS. (1) Journal: published in JAMA, not The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. (2) Year: 2020, not 2025 — it does not belong to a 2025 review except as background. (3) DIRECTION: the submission claims surgery gave 'significantly superior short-term functional outcomes and faster return to activity at 3 months'. FISH did not show a clinically important functional advantage for surgery; its substantive finding is the 14 of 44 braced patients who needed secondary surgery and the worse outcomes in that crossover group. Rewritten around the healing and crossover data, which is the honest argument for early fixation. Also corrected 'multicenter study' to a two-centre randomised trial, and 82 patients stated so the reader knows how small it is.

title: An AI Care Aid for Perioperative Patient Questions in Joint Arthroplasty (HSS and Aidify)
journal: The Journal of Arthroplasty / AAHKS Annual Meeting
breakthrough: HSS surgeons trained a custom-tailored AI agent on their own surgical protocols so that hip and knee replacement patients received answers reflecting their surgeon's actual instructions rather than generic content. A prospective observational pilot used a two-phase design — a 10-patient a priori cohort followed by 30 further patients undergoing primary THA or TKA — with access during the preoperative period and early recovery. Patients rated the responses highly for usefulness, understandability and completeness, and accessed the tool easily.
impact: A demonstration that protocol-specific tuning is what makes a perioperative chatbot acceptable to patients, and an early template for how such a tool would be evaluated before deployment.
practical: Treat this as feasibility, not effectiveness. 40 patients, and the endpoints were acceptability and perceived quality of answers. It did not measure emergency department visits, clinic call volume, protocol adherence or any clinical outcome, and it did not test the tool as a triage instrument — so it cannot yet be offered as a way to reduce unnecessary contacts.
link: Journal of Arthroplasty — AI-powered care aid for perioperative inquiries in joint arthroplasty

verify.status: corrected — real pilot, the claimed benefits were not measured
verify.note: Real: HSS partnered with Aidify on a custom-tailored AI agent, presented at AAHKS and published in The Journal of Arthroplasty as 'Evaluating the Utility and Acceptability of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Care Aid for Perioperative Patient Inquiries in Joint Arthroplasty Surgery'. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Scale and design: a prospective observational pilot of 40 patients (10 a priori plus 30), which the submission does not convey when it says the platform was 'validated'. (2) The submission's practical claim — 'reduces unnecessary emergency room visits and clinic calls while improving patient compliance' — was not an outcome of this study; the endpoints were usefulness, understandability, completeness and ease of access. Removed and replaced with what was measured. 'Triage' also removed: the study did not test triage.

title: Platelet-Rich Plasma as an Adjunct in Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus
breakthrough: A systematic review of 35 studies — 8 clinical and 27 preclinical — examined platelet-rich plasma in osteochondral lesions of the talus. PRP was most often studied as an adjunct to bone marrow stimulation, and 4 of the 5 studies making that comparison reported statistically significant improvements in pain and function over bone marrow stimulation alone. The cartilage-quality rationale comes from the preclinical work, where PRP and bone marrow aspirate concentrate increase chondrocyte proliferation and synthetic capacity and blunt the catabolic effect of an inflamed joint.
impact: Gives foot and ankle surgeons a defensible reason to add point-of-care biologics at the time of bone marrow stimulation, while being explicit that the reason is mechanistic and the clinical evidence is thin.
practical: Reasonable as an adjunct when PRP is already available in theatre; not a substitute for adequate lesion preparation or for addressing malalignment and instability. Weigh the evidence honestly with the patient: 8 clinical studies, mostly small and not randomised, is a signal, not a standard of care, and there is no agreed PRP preparation — leucocyte-rich and leucocyte-poor formulations behave differently.
link: Systematic review — PRP in osteochondral lesions of the talus

verify.status: corrected — journal not confirmed, and the level of evidence was overstated
verify.note: A December 2025 systematic review does exist — 'The Role of Platelet-Rich Plasma in Treating Osteochondral Lesions of the Talus: A Systematic Review of Clinical and Preclinical Evidence', 35 studies (8 clinical, 27 preclinical), with 4 of 5 studies of PRP added to bone marrow stimulation reporting significant pain and function gains. TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) Journal: I could not confirm JBJS Reviews as the venue, so the journal field states the study type instead of naming a journal that may be wrong. (2) The submission says it 'establishes high-level evidence supporting biologic augmentation' and 'enhanced hyaline-like cartilage repair'. Eight mostly small non-randomised clinical studies is not high-level evidence, and the cartilage-quality claim rests on preclinical and proof-of-concept work. Rewritten to separate what the clinical studies showed from what the bench work suggests, and the leucocyte-rich versus leucocyte-poor variability added since it is a live confounder in this literature.

title: Prior Authorization Delays Total Hip Arthroplasty Without Reducing Cost
breakthrough: The first study to quantify the time and cost of obtaining prior authorization for THA examined patients having unilateral primary THA for end-stage hip osteoarthritis under a single commercial payor from January 2020 to December 2022, with HOOS-JR and SF-12 physical component scores recorded preoperatively and at 6 months. Prior authorization was associated with significantly longer waits before surgery and lower preoperative functional scores, and it did not function as a cost-saving measure. A parallel AAHKS membership survey found members reporting high administrative burden (93%), negative clinical consequences (87%) and delays in timely access (96%), most often triggered by a requirement that non-operative treatment had not been tried for long enough.
impact: Gives orthopaedic advocacy an outcome measure rather than an anecdote: the patient reaches the operating room in worse condition, and the payer does not save money.
practical: Refer early and document non-operative treatment explicitly and with dates, since the commonest denial reason is that conservative care was not tried long enough. Note the limits of the data — one commercial payor, one institution, 6-month follow-up — and note what it does not contain: this study did not report opioid use, so a claim that prior authorization increases preoperative opioid consumption cannot be supported from it.
link: AAOS 2025 — prior authorization does not reduce costs for total hip arthroplasty

verify.status: corrected — one claimed finding is not in the study
verify.note: Real, presented at the 2025 AAOS Annual Meeting; the longer wait times and lower preoperative functional scores are accurate, and the headline finding — that prior authorization was not an effective cost-saving measure — was missing from the submission and has been added. CORRECTION: the submission asserts 'increased preoperative opioid use'. No opioid endpoint appears in this study; its patient-reported measures were HOOS-JR and SF-12 PCS. That claim has been removed and the entry says explicitly that it cannot be supported, because it is the kind of plausible detail that gets repeated once written down. Also corrected 'multi-institutional': the study describes a single commercial payor cohort.
